# Two-Dimensional Grid DP {#sec-gd}

::: {.callout-note title="Sources"}
**`dp_book` ch. 3** (the grid as a DAG, memory and prefix sums, an extra index, combining tables, two-index grids, then path counting and richer moves). This chapter starts from the grid-path pattern of the introduction (@sec-dpi-p3, especially @sec-dpi-p3-unique and @sec-dpi-p3-minpath) and from the look-back lesson (@sec-od-look). The state is no longer one index on a line. It is a cell, and the moves decide which cells that cell is allowed to read.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="What you will be able to do"}
- Model a grid process as a DAG of cells, pick a fill order that respects the arrows, and spot when a cycle forces a graph algorithm.
- Fit a grid DP into memory: two rolling rows, an in-place row, and a compact table of choices when the path itself has to be written out.
- Add a coordinate to a cell (steps, a remainder, a balance, a direction) and estimate the cost before filling the table.
- Combine a forward table and a backward table to answer "through this cell" and "meet here".
- Run a grid DP backwards when the requirement is decided by the future, and synchronise two walkers on anti-diagonals.
- Compute a shape quantity — a largest square, a largest rectangle, a count of all-ones submatrices — from a cell-local transition and a 2D prefix sum.
:::


## Why this matters

@sec-od kept one index and let it read many earlier cells. This chapter adds the second index back, as in the grid paths of @sec-dpi-p3, and then asks what else a cell can carry: richer moves, a direction of fill that runs backwards, a second walker, a shape anchored at the cell.

Unique Paths II (@sec-dpi-p3-unique) and Minimum Path Sum (@sec-dpi-p3-minpath) both move only right or down. The fill order is then obvious: row by row, left to right, because each cell reads the cell above it and the cell to its left. The look-back lesson (@sec-od-look) asked, for a fixed index on a line, which earlier indices it reads. A grid asks the same question of a cell. The answer is no longer a fixed pair of neighbours.

A queen that slides until a wall, a falling path that may land in any other column, two people who must share exactly one cell, a path that has to spell a balanced bracket string: each of these is still a DP on cells. What changes is the set of cells a cell reads, how much of the path the future still needs to know, and whether one table is enough. Draw an arrow from each cell to the cells it depends on. The DP is valid when those arrows form a DAG, and the fill order has to respect every arrow. If an arrow can run backwards, there is no order, and the problem is a shortest path.

## Lesson 1: the grid is a DAG {#sec-gd-dag}

The move set fixes the arrows, and the arrows fix the order. Six situations cover the grids in this chapter.

| Moves into $(r, c)$ come from | Fill order | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| up, left | rows downward, columns left to right | a path to the bottom-right (@sec-dpi-p3) |
| down, right, down-right | rows upward, columns right to left | "from here to the end" |
| the whole previous row | row by row; order inside the row is free | a falling path |
| the previous column | column by column, left to right | every move goes right |
| two walkers with $r_1 + c_1 = r_2 + c_2$ | one anti-diagonal $r + c = t$ at a time | two paths that stay in step |
| any neighbour, and nothing else increases | no order | a cycle: BFS, 0-1 BFS, or Dijkstra |

Two orders are not "rows" or "columns", and both are still DAGs.

**By value.** "Step to a neighbour with a strictly larger value" allows all four directions, and it still has no cycle: the value rises along every path. Process the cells in increasing order of value, or let memoised recursion discover that order. On

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 9 & 9 & 4 \\ 6 & 6 & 8 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

the path $1 \to 2 \to 6 \to 9$ is a valid order. A smaller value is never waiting on a larger one.

**By time.** "Any direction, at most $T$ moves" cycles in the grid, and the state $(t, r, c)$ does not: $t$ strictly increases. The grid is copied once per time step. The outer loop is the layer.

If a walker may step to any of the four neighbours, with no budget and no monotone quantity, cell $A$ can depend on cell $B$ and $B$ on $A$. No fill order exists. Unit costs are a BFS, costs in $\{0, 1\}$ are a 0-1 BFS, and non-negative costs are Dijkstra. The trap is to run the right/down DP on a statement that also allows up or left. It passes every sample whose optimum happens to be monotone, and it fails on the first detour. Before writing the table, name the quantity that every allowed move increases: the row, the column, $r + c$, the time, or the value.

Four checks, with the order each one forces:

1. Down, down-left, down-right: every move enters the next row, so the rows go top to bottom.
2. Right, up-right, down-right: every move enters the next column, so the columns go left to right.
3. Right, down, and left, even with "not the same cell twice in a row": left and right inside one row form a cycle. That is not a plain grid DP.
4. Any knight move, exactly $k$ of them: the state is $(t, r, c)$ for $t = 0..k$.

## Lesson 2: memory and prefix sums {#sec-gd-mem}

A grid DP has $mn$ states. At $m = n = 5000$ that is $2.5 \cdot 10^7$ cells: 100 MB of 32-bit integers, 200 MB of 64-bit integers. Most of these transitions read only the previous row.

**Two rolling rows.** If row $r$ reads only row $r - 1$, keep `prev` and `cur` and swap them. This is the safe default.

**One row, updated in place.** With up and left only, one array is enough, the same trick as the grid paths of @sec-dpi-p3. When column $c$ is updated, `row[c]` still holds the value from above and `row[c - 1]` already holds the new value to the left. The up-left neighbour is the value that was overwritten one step earlier. Save it before the write:

```text
tmp = row[c]
row[c] = f(row[c], row[c - 1], diag)
diag = tmp
```

`diag` is the old `row[c - 1]`, which is about to become the up-left of the next cell. Adding that third neighbour without the variable reads a value from the wrong row.

**Roll the smaller side.** A grid of $10^6 \times 5$ does not want a rolling array of length $10^6$. When the arrows allow it, iterate so that the rolling array has length $\min(m, n)$.

A rolling array throws the old rows away. If the path has to be printed, keep a separate choice table of $mn$ bytes ("came from up / left / diagonal") and roll the values. At $5000 \times 5000$ that is 25 MB of choices instead of 200 MB of 64-bit values.

| Grid | Full table, 64-bit | Two rows | Choices, 1 byte |
|---|---|---|---|
| $1000 \times 1000$ | 8 MB | 16 KB | 1 MB |
| $5000 \times 5000$ | 200 MB | 80 KB | 25 MB |
| $10^4 \times 10^4$ | 800 MB, too much | 160 KB | 100 MB |
| $(t, r, c)$ at $50^3$ | 1 MB | — | — |

**A rectangle sum is itself a small DP.** Many grid problems ask for the sum inside a rectangle over and over. Let $P[r][c]$ be the sum of $a[i][j]$ over $i < r$ and $j < c$:

$$
P[r+1][c+1] = a[r][c] + P[r][c+1] + P[r+1][c] - P[r][c].
$$

The last term is subtracted because the top-left block was added twice. The sum of rows $r_1..r_2$ and columns $c_1..c_2$, inclusive, undoes the same overlap:

$$
P[r_2+1][c_2+1] - P[r_1][c_2+1] - P[r_2+1][c_1] + P[r_1][c_1].
$$

def prefix_sum(a):
    m, n = len(a), len(a[0])
    P = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
    for r in range(m):
        for c in range(n):
            P[r + 1][c + 1] = a[r][c] + P[r][c + 1] + P[r + 1][c] - P[r][c]
    def rect(r1, c1, r2, c2):
        return P[r2 + 1][c2 + 1] - P[r1][c2 + 1] - P[r2 + 1][c1] + P[r1][c1]
    return rect

def add_rect(diff, r1, c1, r2, c2, v):
    diff[r1][c1] += v
    diff[r2 + 1][c2 + 1] += v
    diff[r1][c2 + 1] -= v
    diff[r2 + 1][c1] -= v

def from_diff(diff):
    m, n = len(diff), len(diff[0])
    g = [[0] * n for _ in range(m)]
    for r in range(m):
        for c in range(n):
            up = g[r - 1][c] if r else 0
            left = g[r][c - 1] if c else 0
            diag = g[r - 1][c - 1] if r and c else 0
            g[r][c] = diff[r][c] + up + left - diag
    return g

def paths_row(g):
    """Right/down counts in one row. A wall writes 0 and cuts both neighbours."""
    H, W = len(g), len(g[0])
    row = [0] * W
    for r in range(H):
        for c in range(W):
            if g[r][c] == "#":
                row[c] = 0
                continue
            if r == 0 and c == 0:
                row[c] = 1
                continue
            up = row[c] if r else 0
            left = row[c - 1] if c else 0
            row[c] = (up + left) % MOD
    return row[-1]

add_rect(_diff, 0, 0, 1, 1, 5)
_back = from_diff(_diff)
assert prefix_sum(_back)(0, 0, 1, 1) == 20 and _back[2][2] == 0
assert paths_row(["....", ".#..", "...."]) == 4

## Lesson 3: an extra index on a cell {#sec-gd-extra}

Two partial paths that end on the same cell must have the same possible futures. Often they do not. One has used more steps, made more turns, or opened more brackets. The cell alone is then not a state, and the missing fact becomes another coordinate.

| Extra coordinate | Range | The rule that forces it |
|---|---|---|
| steps used or left | $0..T$ | at most $T$ moves, in any direction |
| sum modulo $k$ | $0..k-1$ | the path sum must be divisible by $k$ |
| bracket balance | $0..\lfloor (m+n)/2 \rfloor$ | the path must spell a valid bracket string |
| last direction | 2 or 4 | a turn has a cost, or two equal moves in a row are forbidden |
| turns so far | $0..k$ | at most $k$ turns, so the count can be capped at $k+1$ |
| the other walker | $0..n-1$ | two paths at once |

The table has $mn$ times the length of that range, and the time multiplies by the number of moves as well. Compute the product before coding. $500 \times 500 \times 1000$ balances is $2.5 \cdot 10^8$ booleans, which is too many. The balance can never exceed the number of cells still to visit, and it has to stay at most $(m+n)/2$ to be closable, which often saves a factor of two to four.

Keep only what the future uses. A sum becomes its remainder. A balance is capped by the cells that remain. "Number of turns" becomes "turns so far, capped at $k+1$" when the question is only "at most $k$". A large count becomes a parity when only the parity matters.

**Paths with exactly $k$ turns.** In an $m \times n$ grid, count the right/down paths from the top-left to the bottom-right that change direction exactly $k$ times. A turn is a switch between a right move and a down move. The state $dp[r][c][t][d]$ is the number of paths that reach $(r, c)$ with $t$ turns so far and last move $d \in \{\mathrm{R}, \mathrm{D}\}$. The same direction keeps $t$. The other direction increases it. With four coordinates, "where can I go from here" is easier to list than "where could I have come from", so the natural writing is a push:

$$
\begin{aligned}
dp[r][c+1][t][\mathrm{R}] &\mathrel{+}= dp[r][c][t][\mathrm{R}] + dp[r][c][t-1][\mathrm{D}],\\
dp[r+1][c][t][\mathrm{D}] &\mathrel{+}= dp[r][c][t][\mathrm{D}] + dp[r][c][t-1][\mathrm{R}].
\end{aligned}
$$

The first move leaves the corner with $t = 0$ in either direction. On a $4 \times 4$ grid the counts by number of turns are $0, 2, 4, 8, 4, 2, 0$. They sum to $\binom{6}{3} = 20$. One turn is the two L-shaped paths. Five turns is the two zigzags `RDRDRD` and `DRDRDR`. No path has 0 turns, because both directions are required, and none has 6, because six moves have only five gaps.

Every move increases $r + c$, so the loops over $t$ and $d$ inside a cell can run in either order. A step coordinate $t$ with moves in all four directions is different: $t$ has to be the outermost loop, because the next layer depends on the whole previous layer and neighbours inside one layer do not depend on each other.

::: {#26304659 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def paths_by_turns(m, n):
    K = m + n
    dp = [[[[0, 0] for _ in range(K)] for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[0][1][0][0] = 1
    dp[1][0][0][1] = 1
    for r in range(m):
        for c in range(n):
            for t in range(K - 1):
                for d in range(2):
                    v = dp[r][c][t][d]
                    if not v:
                        continue
                    if c + 1 < n:
                        dp[r][c + 1][t + (d == 1)][0] += v
                    if r + 1 < m:
                        dp[r + 1][c][t + (d == 0)][1] += v
    return [dp[m - 1][n - 1][t][0] + dp[m - 1][n - 1][t][1] for t in range(7)]

assert paths_by_turns(4, 4) == [0, 2, 4, 8, 4, 2, 0]
assert sum(paths_by_turns(4, 4)) == 20
```
:::


## Lesson 4: combining two tables {#sec-gd-comb}

One table answers "what is the best, or how many, from the start to here?" Several questions need both sides of a cell. Which cells lie on some optimal path, or on every one? How many paths pass through $(r, c)$, and how many avoid it? If every cell might be blocked, what is the new answer, for every cell, without rerunning the DP? Where should two people meet?

Every start-to-goal path through $X$ splits there into a prefix and a suffix, and the two halves are chosen independently. Any prefix can be glued to any suffix:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{best path through } X &= f[X] + b[X] - v[X],\\
\text{number of paths through } X &= F[X] \cdot B[X].
\end{aligned}
$$

Sums add and counts multiply. The value $v[X]$ is subtracted once because both halves include the cell. A right/down path through $X$ stays in the rectangle from the start to $X$ and then in the rectangle from $X$ to the goal, so each table is an ordinary grid DP on its own rectangle.

**Forward.** $f[r][c] = v[r][c] + \max(f[r-1][c], f[r][c-1])$, filled from the top-left. **Backward.** $b[r][c] = v[r][c] + \max(b[r+1][c], b[r][c+1])$, filled from the bottom-right. On

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

the best path sums to 14. A cell lies on some optimal path exactly when $f + b - v = 14$. Cell $(1, 1)$ has $f = 5$, $b = 10$, $v = 1$, and $5 + 10 - 1 = 14$. Cell $(0, 3)$ gives at best $7 + 6 - 2 = 11$, so it lies on none. Following parent pointers recovers one optimal path. The combination, read at every cell, is the union of all of them.

A right/down path crosses each anti-diagonal $r + c = \text{const}$ exactly once. A marked cell is on every optimal path when it is the only marked cell on its anti-diagonal. Here the anti-diagonals $0, 1, 3, 5$ each contain one marked cell, so $(0, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 3)$ are unavoidable. Diagonals $2$ and $4$ contain two marked cells each, so the optimal paths still have a choice there.

The counting version uses the same two sweeps with $+$ instead of $\max$. On an empty $3 \times 4$ grid there are 10 paths. The centre cell $(1, 1)$ is reached in 2 ways and left in 3, so $2 \cdot 3 = 6$ paths use it, and $10 - 6 = 4$ avoid it. Along any anti-diagonal the through-counts sum to the total, because each path crosses it once: $4 + 6 = 10$ on $r + c = 1$, and $1 + 6 + 3 = 10$ on $r + c = 2$. Under a modulus the sums agree modulo $10^9+7$. If $F \cdot B$ fails the test, one of the two tables is wrong.

Blocking one cell is the complement, $\text{total} - F[X] \cdot B[X]$. Both factors are below the modulus, so the product fits in a 64-bit integer and not in a 32-bit one. The difference of two reduced values can be negative: add the modulus before the final reduction. With the two tables in hand, every "what if $X$ were blocked?" is one arithmetic operation. Rerunning the DP per cell is $O((mn)^2)$.

Several blocked cells are not several subtractions. A path through two of them would be subtracted twice. That inclusion-exclusion, organised as a DP over the walls, is what a $10^5 \times 10^5$ grid with a few thousand walls needs. The state moves from "every cell" to "every interesting cell".

The combination is valid only when any prefix can be glued to any suffix. It fails when the state carries history across the cut: "no cell visited twice" with moves in all directions, or a budget on the total number of turns. Then both sides need the extra coordinate, or the trick does not apply.

Two walkers with different corners meet in one cell, and each walker's route splits into a half before the meeting and a half after it. That is four tables, one from each corner. The meeting cell itself is handled the way the statement says: counted once, counted twice, or not counted. @sec-gd-p1-work is that combination, with only two legal ways to cross the cell.

def best_through(a):
    H, W = len(a), len(a[0])
    neg = -(10**18)
    f = [[0] * W for _ in range(H)]
    b = [[0] * W for _ in range(H)]
    for r in range(H):
        for c in range(W):
            best = 0 if (r, c) == (0, 0) else neg
            if r:
                best = max(best, f[r - 1][c])
            if c:
                best = max(best, f[r][c - 1])
            if (r, c) == (0, 0):
                best = 0
            f[r][c] = a[r][c] + best
    for r in range(H - 1, -1, -1):
        for c in range(W - 1, -1, -1):
            best = 0 if (r, c) == (H - 1, W - 1) else neg
            if r + 1 < H:
                best = max(best, b[r + 1][c])
            if c + 1 < W:
                best = max(best, b[r][c + 1])
            if (r, c) == (H - 1, W - 1):
                best = 0
            b[r][c] = a[r][c] + best
    opt = f[H - 1][W - 1]
    on = [(r, c) for r in range(H) for c in range(W) if f[r][c] + b[r][c] - a[r][c] == opt]
    return opt, on

def count_tables(g):
    H, W = len(g), len(g[0])
    F = [[0] * W for _ in range(H)]
    B = [[0] * W for _ in range(H)]
    for r in range(H):
        for c in range(W):
            if g[r][c] == "#":
                continue
            if r == 0 and c == 0:
                F[r][c] = 1
                continue
            F[r][c] = ((F[r - 1][c] if r else 0) + (F[r][c - 1] if c else 0)) % MOD
    for r in range(H - 1, -1, -1):
        for c in range(W - 1, -1, -1):
            if g[r][c] == "#":
                continue
            if r == H - 1 and c == W - 1:
                B[r][c] = 1
                continue
            B[r][c] = ((B[r + 1][c] if r + 1 < H else 0) + (B[r][c + 1] if c + 1 < W else 0)) % MOD
    return F, B

## Lesson 5: two indices are still a grid {#sec-gd-two}

So far the grid was the input. Any DP whose state is a pair $(i, j)$ lives in a two-dimensional table, and the arrows, the fill order, the rolling rows, and the forward/backward split apply unchanged. Three families come back in every later chapter.

**Two sequences.** $dp[i][j]$ is the answer for the prefixes $s[0..i)$ and $t[0..j)$. The cell reads up (drop a character of $s$), left (drop a character of $t$), and up-left (drop both). That is a right/down grid with one extra arrow. The longest common subsequence of `GRID` and `RIDGE` is 3, the letters `RID`. A match takes the diagonal and adds one. A mismatch takes the better of up and left. The `G` matched against the `G` of `RIDGE` cannot be extended: the only letter after that `G` is `E`. The fill order is rows, then columns. Two rolling rows hold the values. Reconstruction walks back from the bottom-right corner.

**Items and a budget.** "Using the first $i$ items, with $k$ of something used" is a grid whose row $i$ depends only on row $i - 1$. Pascal's triangle is the smallest one: $C[i][k] = C[i-1][k] + C[i-1][k-1]$, skip the item or take it. One array of length $k + 1$, updated downwards, keeps $C[k-1]$ on the old row. That is the 0/1 direction of the loop. $C[4][2] = 3 + 3 = 6$.

**Intervals.** The state is a contiguous piece $s[l..r]$. Only the triangle $l \le r$ is used, and $dp[l][r]$ reads shorter intervals: $[l+1, r]$, $[l, r-1]$, $[l+1, r-1]$, or a split. In the grid those cells lie to the left and below, so "rows top to bottom" is the wrong order. Fill by increasing length, or by decreasing $l$ and increasing $r$. The substrings of `abaab` that are palindromes are the five single letters, `aba`, `aa`, and `baab`: eight of them. A length of 1 or 2 needs only the two ends equal. A longer one also needs the strict inside to be a palindrome, which is the previous diagonal.

| State | Reads | Fill order | Memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| a grid cell $(r, c)$ | the neighbours the moves name | the move set | rolling rows |
| two prefixes $(i, j)$ | $(i-1, j)$, $(i, j-1)$, $(i-1, j-1)$ | rows, then columns | two rows |
| items $\times$ budget $(i, k)$ | row $i-1$ only | rows; $k$ downwards if the row is updated in place | one row |
| an interval $(l, r)$ | shorter intervals inside $[l, r]$ | by length, or $l$ downward and $r$ upward | the whole triangle |

The habit is the picture. Whenever the state has two indices, sketch the table and draw the arrows of one cell. The picture says the order, how far back the arrows reach, and how to walk back from the answer cell.

def lcs(s, t):
    dp = [[0] * (len(t) + 1) for _ in range(len(s) + 1)]
    for i in range(1, len(s) + 1):
        for j in range(1, len(t) + 1):
            if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
            else:
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    return dp[-1][-1]

def choose(n, k):
    C = [0] * (k + 1)
    C[0] = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(min(i, k), 0, -1):
            C[j] += C[j - 1]
    return C[k]

def pal_count(s):
    n, count = len(s), 0
    pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for length in range(1, n + 1):
        for left in range(n - length + 1):
            right = left + length - 1
            pal[left][right] = s[left] == s[right] and (length <= 2 or pal[left + 1][right - 1])
            count += pal[left][right]
    return count

## Pattern 1: path counting and combining tables {#sec-gd-p1}

**Where we are.** The lessons showed that a grid is a DAG of cells and that a cell can carry an extra index. The patterns climb one idea at a time: count paths and combine a forward table with a backward one (this pattern), let a cell read a larger or stranger set of predecessors (Pattern 2), fill backwards when the requirement is set by the future, or add a move counter when the moves have cycles (Pattern 3), move two walkers on one clock (Pattern 4), and finally measure a shape anchored at the cell instead of a path that ends there (Pattern 5).

**Recognise it.** The moves only go forward, so the cells are a DAG. The question is a count of paths, usually modulo $10^9+7$, or a best path value, and it mentions a cell in the middle: paths through $X$, paths avoiding $X$, the cells on some optimal path, two people who meet in exactly one cell. A wall is a cell that contributes nothing. A move that may cover a whole ray, a queen that cannot jump, is the same table with the ray summed by a running total.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
On a road, $F[r][c] = F[r-1][c] + F[r][c-1]$ modulo $10^9+7$, and a wall is 0. The backward table reads the cell below and the cell to the right, filled from its own corner. Paths through $X$ are $F[X] \cdot B[X]$. The best path forced through $X$ is $f[X] + b[X] - a[X]$.

A queen move sums three rays, left, up, and up-left, each one stopped by the first wall. One running sum per ray makes the cell $O(1)$, and a wall resets all three sums. Two walkers who meet once need one table per corner. The shared cell is counted the way the statement says, which may be not at all.
:::

Each table is $O(HW)$. A few tables are still $O(HW)$. Summing a ray cell by cell is $O(HW(H+W))$, which at $2000 \times 2000$ is about $10^{10}$ additions. The memoised recursion is safe on depth: every call moves closer to the start, so the stack is at most $H + W - 1$. The table is still the one to write, and it shrinks to a rolling row (@sec-gd-mem).

Leave this pattern when every move can go backwards: the count of paths is then infinite or needs a different definition, and the shortest path is a graph search (@sec-gd-dag). Leave it when the two walkers share many cells and a shared cell must be counted once: the halves are no longer independent. Leave it when the grid is $10^5 \times 10^5$ with a few walls: the table does not fit, and the state becomes the walls.

### Problem: Queen on grid {#sec-gd-p1-queen}

::: {.p-statement}
A grid has $H$ rows and $W$ columns. Each cell is a road (`.`) or a wall (`#`). A queen starts on the top-left road. In one move it travels any number of cells right, down, or diagonally down-right, lands on a road, and never jumps a wall. Count the journeys from the top-left to the bottom-right, modulo $10^9+7$. Two journeys differ when, after some move, the queen stands on different cells.

$2 \le H, W \le 2000$, and both corners are roads. On `...` / `.#.` / `...` the answer is 10. On `...#` / `....` / `..#.` / `....` the answer is 84. On an empty $8 \times 10$ the answer is 13701937.

Source: [AC abc183_e · Queen on Grid](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc183/tasks/abc183_e){.solved}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
An empty $8 \times 10$ already has 13701937 journeys, an empty $20 \times 20$ about $1.6 \cdot 10^{18}$, and an empty $30 \times 30$ about $2.1 \cdot 10^{28}$. The count has to be built without listing the journeys, and it has to be reduced modulo $10^9+7$.

This is not Unique Paths with a diagonal step. A move of length 2 is one move, different from two moves of length 1. Counting only the three neighbouring cells counts king walks: 13 on an empty $3 \times 3$, where the queen has 22, and 4 on the first sample, where the queen has 10. On the three samples the one-step count gives 4, 23, and 224143.

The last move into $(r, c)$ started on one of three rays pointing back from that cell: left, up, or up-left. Every road on the ray, up to and not including the first wall, is a possible origin. The wall and everything behind it are not, because the queen cannot jump. Different origins are different journeys, so the counts add. Summing the rays directly is too slow. A sum along a line is a prefix (@sec-od-look, and the rectangle sums of @sec-gd-mem). Keep one running sum per direction, extend it by $dp[r][c]$ after the cell, and reset it to 0 at a wall.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $dp[r][c]$ = ways to reach $(r, c)$ from $(0, 0)$, modulo $10^9+7$. $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are the sums of $dp$ along the row to the left, the column upward, and the diagonal up-left, each one stopping before the first wall.
- **Transition.** A wall sets all four to 0. A road takes $dp[r][c] = X[r][c-1] + Y[r-1][c] + Z[r-1][c-1]$, missing cells as 0, and then extends each running sum by $dp[r][c]$.
- **Base.** $dp[0][0] = 1$, the journey that has not moved. **Answer.** $dp[H-1][W-1]$. **Order.** Row by row, left to right: the left, upper, and upper-left cells are ready.

def queen_rec(g):
    H, W = len(g), len(g[0])

    def f(r, c):
        if r == 0 and c == 0:
            return 1
        total = 0
        for dr, dc in ((0, -1), (-1, 0), (-1, -1)):
            k = 1
            while True:
                pr, pc = r + dr * k, c + dc * k
                if pr < 0 or pc < 0 or g[pr][pc] == "#":

                total += f(pr, pc)
                k += 1
        return total % MOD

    return f(H - 1, W - 1)

### Problem: Working out {#sec-gd-p1-work}

::: {.p-statement}
A gym is an $n \times m$ grid. Working out in cell $(i, j)$ burns $a[i][j]$ calories. Iahub starts at the top-left and must finish at the bottom-right, moving only right or down. Iahubina starts at the bottom-left and must finish at the top-right, moving only right or up. Their paths meet in exactly one cell, and at that cell neither of them works out. Every other cell on either path is worked out once. Maximise the total calories.

$3 \le n, m \le 1000$ and $0 \le a[i][j] \le 10^5$. On a $3 \times 3$ of 100s with a 1 in the centre the answer is 800.

Source: [CF 429B · Working out](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/429/B){.solved rating="1600"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"Let Iahub take a best path, then give Iahubina her best path that meets it once" loses. On

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 7 & 1 & 5 \\ 5 & 1 & 6 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 8 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Iahub's best path alone is worth 25 and takes the 7, the 6, and the 8. Iahubina then has one place to cross it, and the best total of that kind is 33. The optimum is 40: Iahub gives up the 6 and they cross on the cheap cell of value 1. The two people interact only through the meeting cell, so the cell is chosen first and each route is optimised around it.

They meet at $X = (i, j)$. Each route splits into a half before $X$ and a half after $X$. That is four right/down or right/up paths, one from each corner:

- $d_1[i][j]$: best sum from the top-left to $(i, j)$, right or down;
- $d_2[i][j]$: best sum from $(i, j)$ to the bottom-right, right or down;
- $d_3[i][j]$: best sum from the bottom-left to $(i, j)$, right or up;
- $d_4[i][j]$: best sum from $(i, j)$ to the top-right, right or up.

Each table includes $a$ at both of its own ends. Iahub enters $X$ from above or from the left and leaves down or right. Iahubina enters from below or from the left and leaves up or right. If they used a common neighbour they would meet twice. Of the 16 local combinations, two survive. In crossing A, Iahub goes left to right and Iahubina goes below to up. In crossing B, Iahub goes above to below and Iahubina goes left to right.

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(i, j) &= d_1[i][j-1] + d_2[i][j+1] + d_3[i+1][j] + d_4[i-1][j],\\
B(i, j) &= d_1[i-1][j] + d_2[i+1][j] + d_3[i][j-1] + d_4[i][j+1].
\end{aligned}
$$

The answer is the maximum of $A$ and $B$ over interior cells. The cell $(i, j)$ is never added: every table is read at a neighbour. Both crossings use all four neighbours, so a border cell cannot be the meeting. The loops run over $1 \le i \le n-2$ and $1 \le j \le m-2$ in 0-based indices, which is also why every $i \pm 1$ and $j \pm 1$ is inside the grid.

On the $3 \times 4$ example the only interior cells are $(1, 1)$ and $(1, 2)$. Crossing A at $(1, 1)$ is $7 + 15 + 4 + 13 = 39$. Crossing B there is $9 + 12 + 6 + 13 = 40$. Crossing B at $(1, 2)$ is the greedy 33. The four numbers in the winning sum are the two people's halves, and the 1 on the meeting cell is in none of them.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **States.** Four tables $d_1..d_4$, each including $a$ at both ends of its own path.
- **Transitions.** $d_1[i][j] = a[i][j] + \max(d_1[i-1][j], d_1[i][j-1])$. $d_2$ reads down and right. $d_3$ reads down and left. $d_4$ reads up and right.
- **Base.** Each table's own corner holds $a$ of that corner. A missing neighbour contributes $-\infty$. Because $a \ge 0$, a 0 in the padding is the same fact.
- **Orders.** $d_1$ rows downward, columns rightward. $d_2$ rows upward, columns leftward. $d_3$ rows upward, columns rightward. $d_4$ rows downward, columns leftward.
- **Answer.** The better of crossings A and B over every interior cell. **Cost.** $O(nm)$ time and four tables. A half-path has at most 1999 cells, so one entry is at most about $2 \cdot 10^8$ and four of them about $8 \cdot 10^8$, inside a 32-bit integer. The sum of four entries wants a 64-bit temporary.
:::

## Pattern 2: richer moves {#sec-gd-p2}

**From fixed neighbours to a predecessor set.** In Pattern 1 a cell read a few neighbours, or a ray summed by a running total. Now the set of cells a cell may be entered from, $P(r, c)$, is whatever the moves say: a whole previous row, three directions with ties to count, or a path whose value depends on the whole string it spells. The one idea is to summarise $P(r, c)$, or add the missing fact as an index.

**Recognise it.** The path is still on a grid, and the steps are not just right and down. The statement says "down-left, down, or down-right", "any column of the next row except this one", "you may also move diagonally", or "the path as a whole must be a valid bracket string". Write $P(r, c)$ for the cells from which $(r, c)$ can be entered. The move set decides the fill order, and a large $P(r, c)$ is usually almost the same set for every cell of the row, so one summary of the previous row answers every cell.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
$dp[r][c] = g[r][c] \otimes \mathrm{COMBINE}_{(r', c') \in P(r, c)} dp[r'][c']$. Fill in any order that writes every cell of $P(r, c)$ before $(r, c)$.

When $P(r, c)$ is the whole previous row, one minimum does every cell. When it is the whole row except column $c$, three numbers do it: the minimum, the column that holds it, and the second minimum, counting a duplicate of the minimum as a real second. A window of columns is the deque of @sec-od-p1-jump6. To count optimal paths, store the pair (best value, number of ways): replace on a strict improvement, add on a tie. An unreachable cell is marked by the value, not by a count of 0. A property of the whole path (a balance, a remainder) is one more index on the cell.
:::

A constant number of neighbours is $O(1)$ per cell, $O(mn)$ for the grid. A previous row of width $n$ is $O(n)$ per cell and $O(mn^2)$ for the grid, until the row summary brings it back to $O(mn)$. An extra index multiplies both the time and the memory by the length of its range. Row-major order is valid only when every predecessor is above, or in the same row and to the left. Moves that go right, up-right, and down-right have a predecessor in the next row. On $[[9, 1, 1], [1, 9, 9], [9, 9, 9]]$, column by column, the minimum is 3. The same recurrence in row-major order never sees the climb, and it returns 11.

Leave this pattern when the moves have costs and run in all four directions: that graph has cycles (@sec-gd-dag). Leave it when the end condition depends on the cells still to come and the natural question is "how much do I need from here": that fill runs backwards. Leave it when two paths must be moved together.

### Problem: Minimum falling path sum II {#sec-gd-p2-fall}

::: {.p-statement}
Given an $n \times n$ integer matrix, choose one element from every row so that no two elements chosen in adjacent rows are in the same column. Return the minimum possible sum.

$1 \le n \le 200$ and every entry is between $-99$ and $99$. On $[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]$ the answer is 13, the cells $1, 5, 7$. On $[[7]]$ the answer is 7.

Source: [LC 1289 · Minimum Falling Path Sum II](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-falling-path-sum-ii/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Read the chosen cells from top to bottom. From column $c'$ in the previous row the next choice may be any column except $c'$. So $P(r, c)$ is the whole previous row except column $c$: $n - 1$ predecessors, not the three of an ordinary falling path. Every move goes down one row, so row-by-row order is valid, and the order inside a row does not matter.

"Take the smallest allowed cell of each row" loses. On $[[1, 2], [1, 10]]$ it takes the 1 in column 0 and is then forced to take 10: total 11. The optimum is $2 + 1 = 3$. A slightly worse first choice keeps the cheap column free.

If the best choice for rows $0..r$ ends in column $c$, its rows $0..r-1$ are a best choice ending in some other column. The cells of one row share almost the same predecessors. The minimum of the previous row, the column that holds it, and the second minimum answer "best except column $c$" in $O(1)$. A second copy of the minimum is a legal other column. This is the same summary as Vacation (@sec-dpi-p4-vacation), with $n$ activities instead of three, and a minimum instead of a maximum.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $dp[r][c]$ = minimum sum of a valid choice for rows $0..r$ that uses column $c$ in row $r$.
- **Transition.** $dp[r][c] = g[r][c] + \min_{c' \ne c} dp[r-1][c']$.
- **Base.** $dp[0][c] = g[0][c]$. **Answer.** $\min_c dp[n-1][c]$. **Order.** Row by row.
- **Cost.** The direct table is $O(n^3)$, fine at $n = 200$. Best and second best are $O(n^2)$ time. The summary of the newest row can be kept in three integers, so the table itself need not be stored. Sums stay inside $\pm 200 \cdot 99$.

### Problem: Number of paths with max score {#sec-gd-p2-score}

::: {.p-statement}
The board is an $n \times n$ array of characters. The top-left cell is `E`, the bottom-right cell is `S`, and every other cell is a digit `1`–`9` or an obstacle `X`. Starting on `S`, you may move up, left, or up-left, never onto an obstacle, until you reach `E`. The score of a path is the sum of the digits it visits. `E` and `S` score 0.

Return the maximum score and the number of paths that achieve it, the count modulo $10^9+7$. If `E` cannot be reached, return `[0, 0]`.

$2 \le n \le 100$. `["E23", "2X2", "12S"]` gives `[7, 1]`. `["E12", "1X1", "21S"]` gives `[4, 2]`. `["E11", "XXX", "11S"]` gives `[0, 0]`.

Source: [LC 1301 · Number of Paths With Max Score](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-paths-with-max-score/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"Step toward the largest digit" loses. On `["E65", "8X4", "75S"]` it takes the 5 to the left of `S`, then the diagonal 8, and scores 13. The best path is `S`, 5, 7, 8, `E`, score 20. The diagonal is short, and a shorter path collects fewer digits.

A path from `S` to `E` by up, left, and up-left, read backwards, is a path from `E` to `S` by down, right, and down-right. The cells and the score are the same. Fill from `E` in ordinary row-major order. The three predecessors of $(r, c)$ are up, left, and up-left, all earlier in that order.

The cell stores a pair. The best score is the best predecessor score plus the digit. The number of ways is the sum of the counts of the predecessors that tie for that score. A worse predecessor contributes nothing. Counts are modulo $10^9+7$, and a reachable cell can have a count that is a multiple of the modulus. Mark an unreachable cell with score $-1$. A real score is at least 0, so $-1$ is not a score, and a count of 0 is not the test.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $(sc[r][c], wy[r][c])$ = the best score of a path between `E` and $(r, c)$, digit included, and the number of such paths modulo $10^9+7$. $sc = -1$ when no path exists.
- **Transition.** Over the predecessors with $sc \ge 0$: keep the best score, and add the counts of the predecessors that match it. Then add the digit. An obstacle, and a cell with no reachable predecessor, stays at $-1$.
- **Base.** $sc[0][0] = 0$, $wy[0][0] = 1$. **Answer.** The pair at $(n-1, n-1)$, or `[0, 0]` when that score is $-1$. **Order.** Row-major.
- **Cost.** $O(n^2)$ time. Two rolling rows are enough, and one is not: the up-left predecessor would already have been overwritten by the cell to the left.

### Problem: Valid parentheses string path {#sec-gd-p2-paren}

::: {.p-statement}
An $m \times n$ grid holds `(` and `)`. A path starts at the top-left, ends at the bottom-right, and moves only right or down. Reading the cells along the path gives a string. Return whether some path gives a valid parentheses string: `()`, or $AB$, or $(A)$ for valid strings $A$ and $B$.

$1 \le m, n \le 100$. On rows `(((`, `)()`, `(()`, `(()` the answer is true. On rows `))`, `((` the answer is false.

Source: [LC 2267 · Check if There Is a Valid Parentheses String Path](https://leetcode.com/problems/check-if-there-is-a-valid-parentheses-string-path/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Let the balance be the number of `(` read so far minus the number of `)`. A string is valid when the balance stays non-negative after every character and finishes at 0. The only fact about the prefix that the future needs is that number, provided it never went negative.

The cell alone is not a state. On rows `(((`, `())` the last cell is entered with balance 3 from above and balance 1 from the left. The last character is `)`, so 3 becomes 2 and 1 becomes 0. Keeping only the largest balance answers false. The true answer is true, along `(())`. Keeping only the smallest non-negative balance fails the other way: on rows `(((((`, `())))` the small balance dies in the closing brackets, and the path that stays on the top row reads `((()))`.

A path has $L = m + n - 1$ characters. If $L$ is odd the answer is false at once. After cell $(r, c)$ there are $\mathrm{rem} = (m-1-r) + (n-1-c)$ characters left, and each can lower the balance by at most one, so any state with balance above $\mathrm{rem}$ can be dropped. In particular every useful balance is at most $\lfloor L/2 \rfloor \le 99$.

Every move increases $r + c$, whatever the balance does. The row-major order of the plain grid stays valid. The balance only adds a column of states to each cell. Sample 1 has $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ paths of length 6, and 4 of them are valid: two read `()(())` and two read `((()))`.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $ok[r][c][b]$ is true when some right/down path to $(r, c)$, the character included, has stayed non-negative and ends at balance $b$.
- **Transition.** $d = +1$ for `(` and $-1$ for `)`. $ok[r][c][b] = ok[r-1][c][b-d] \lor ok[r][c-1][b-d]$, and only for $0 \le b \le \mathrm{rem}(r, c)$.
- **Base.** The corner is balance 1 if it is `(`, and nothing if it is `)`. **Answer.** $ok[m-1][n-1][0]$. False at once when $m + n - 1$ is odd. **Order.** Row-major.
- **Cost.** At most about $10^6$ states. One bit mask per cell turns the column of booleans into an OR and a shift.
:::

::: {.form-next}
One cell is a set of balances. Bit $b$ is set when balance $b$ is possible. The transition is an OR of the two neighbours, then a shift: left by one for `(`, right by one for `)`. ## Pattern 3: backward and layered DP {#sec-gd-p3}

**From the past to the future.** Every table so far summarised the path behind a cell. Some questions are decided by the path **ahead**: how much health you need on entering a room depends on the rooms still to come. Turn the fill around and the summary becomes one number again. When the moves have cycles, a move counter that only grows plays the same role and gives the order.

**Recognise it.** The number you have to fix at the start depends on what happens later on the path, or the moves point in every direction and only a counter (moves left, fuel, time, a strictly larger value) makes the states a DAG. A forward summary of "health so far" keeps two numbers that do not dominate each other. A suffix often has one number: the least health you must hold on entering the cell, or the number of ways to finish from here with $k$ moves left.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
**Backward.** $need(r,c)$ is the least value on entering $(r,c)$ that can still finish. For a dungeon,

$$
need(r,c) = \max\big(1,\ \min(need(r{+}1,c),\ need(r,c{+}1)) - g[r][c]\big),
$$

with a virtual cell after the target seeded at $1$ and every other outside cell at $+\infty$. Fill rows from the target back to the start, and each row from right to left. One rolling row is enough.

**Layered.** Moves may go up, down, left, and right, but every move increases a counter $t$. Then

$$
dp[t{+}1][r'][c'] \mathrel{+}= dp[t][r][c]
$$

for each legal step, and a step that leaves the grid is an event you count rather than a cell you store. Layer $t{+}1$ is a different array from layer $t$.
:::

**Complexity.** The backward table is $O(mn)$ time and $O(n)$ memory. The layered count is $O(K \cdot mn)$ time and $O(mn)$ memory with two layers. A memo key that forgets $t$ is a different problem, and on a cyclic grid it does not even terminate. If nothing on the walk strictly increases, the search is BFS or Dijkstra, not a fill order.

### Problem: Dungeon game {#sec-gd-p3-dung}

::: {.p-statement}
A knight starts in the top-left room and must reach the princess in the bottom-right room, moving only right or down. A negative room takes that much health, a positive room restores it, and health must stay at least $1$ after every room, including the princess's. Return the least starting health. Here $1 \le m, n \le 200$ and each room is between $-1000$ and $1000$.

Source: [LC 174 · Dungeon Game](https://leetcode.com/problems/dungeon-game/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
For one fixed path the answer is easy: if the prefix sums bottom out at $L$, the knight needs $\max(1, 1 - L)$. Choosing the path is the hard part. The path that gains the most on the first sample, down, down, right, right, ends $28$ up but dipped to $-7$ and needs $8$. The path right, right, down, down only gains $-6$, yet its lowest prefix is $-6$, so it needs $7$. Health at the end is not what you protect. Health on the way is, and that is a property of the suffix.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $need(r,c)$ = least health on entering $(r,c)$, before the room is applied, such that some right/down path from there reaches the princess alive.
- **Transition.** After the room the health is $h + g[r][c]$, and it must cover the cheaper successor and the knight must be alive on entry: $need(r,c) = \max(1,\ \min(need(r{+}1,c),\ need(r,c{+}1)) - g[r][c])$.
- **Base.** The cell under the princess and the cell to her right are $1$. Every other padding cell is $+\infty$. **Answer.** $need(0,0)$. **Order.** Bottom to top, right to left.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

    m, n = len(dungeon), len(dungeon[0])

### Problem: Out of boundary paths {#sec-gd-p3-out}

::: {.p-statement}
A ball starts at `(startRow, startColumn)` on an $m \times n$ grid. Each move steps to an adjacent cell, and a step that crosses the border removes the ball. Count the move sequences of length at most `maxMove` that take the ball out, modulo $10^9+7$. Here $m, n \le 50$ and `maxMove` $\le 50$.

Source: [LC 576 · Out of Boundary Paths](https://leetcode.com/problems/out-of-boundary-paths/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Right then left returns to the start, so a table indexed only by the cell has no fill order and the count of walks is infinite. The move budget is what grows. After $t$ moves the ball is at one cell, still inside, or it has already left. Leaving is the event you add; staying is the mass you push into the next layer.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $dp[t][r][c]$ = sequences of length $t$ that are still inside and end at $(r, c)$. The backward view is $f(r, c, k)$ = ways to leave from $(r, c)$ with at most $k$ moves left.
- **Transition.** From $(r, c)$, each of the four steps either adds $dp[t][r][c]$ to the answer (the step left the grid) or adds it into $dp[t{+}1][r'][c']$.
- **Base.** $dp[0][\mathrm{start}] = 1$. Inside with no moves left is $0$. Already outside is $1$. **Answer.** The sum of every exit found while pushing layers $0, \ldots, \mathrm{maxMove}-1$.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

def boundary_rec(m, n, max_move, start_row, start_col):
    def go(r, c, left):
        if r < 0 or r >= m or c < 0 or c >= n:

        if left == 0:

        return (go(r - 1, c, left - 1) + go(r + 1, c, left - 1)

## Pattern 4: two walkers {#sec-gd-p4}

**From one path to two.** Each DP so far moved one walker. When two paths collect from the same grid and a shared cell pays once, their choices interact, and optimising them one after the other is a greedy that loses. Move both on one clock, so the state holds both positions at the same time, and the shared cell is a test on that state.

**Recognise it.** Two paths collect values, and a cell both of them visit is paid once. "Go to the corner and come back" is the same set of cells as two walks that both go to the corner. Optimising one path, erasing it, and optimising again is a greedy: on a $3\times 4$ of cherries it collects $5$ when $6$ is possible, and the best single path there is unique, so a tie-break does not save it.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Move both walkers on one clock. After $t$ right-or-down steps, each walker stands on the anti-diagonal $r + c = t$, so the column is $t - r$ and the state is $(t, r_1, r_2)$.

$$
dp[t][r_1][r_2] = g[r_1][t - r_1] + [r_1 \ne r_2]\, g[r_2][t - r_2] + \max_{d_1, d_2 \in \{0, 1\}} dp[t - 1][r_1 - d_1][r_2 - d_2].
$$

A thorn makes the state $-\infty$, not $0$. The public answer is $\max(0, dp)$ at the far corner. Robots that both drop one row per turn use $(r, c_1, c_2)$ and nine moves, and they share a cell exactly when $c_1 = c_2$.
:::

**Complexity.** Diagonal walkers are $O((m + n) m^2)$ time, or half of that if you store only $r_1 \le r_2$ and read every predecessor at $(\min, \max)$. Two layers bring the memory to $O(m^2)$. Row-synchronised robots are $O(m n^2)$ time and $O(n^2)$ memory. The rows on diagonal $t$ of an $m \times n$ grid are $\max(0, t - n + 1)$ through $\min(m - 1, t)$.

### Problem: Cherry pickup {#sec-gd-p4-cherry}

::: {.p-statement}
An $n \times n$ grid holds cherries ($1$), empty rooms ($0$), and thorns ($-1$). Start at $(0, 0)$, walk to $(n - 1, n - 1)$ by right and down steps, then walk back to $(0, 0)$ by left and up steps. A cherry is collected once, the first time a walk enters its room. Return the most cherries you can collect, or $0$ if the round trip is impossible. Here $n \le 50$.

Source: [LC 741 · Cherry Pickup](https://leetcode.com/problems/cherry-pickup/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Read the return trip backwards and it is a second right/down walk from the start to the corner, on the same cells. The score depends only on the set of cells, so the round trip is two forward walkers. They can share a cell only at the tick $t = r + c$, which in the state is the test $r_1 = r_2$. That is why one equality pays the cell once.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $dp[t][r_1][r_2]$, with $r_1 \le r_2$, is the most cherries two walkers can have collected on reaching $(r_1, t - r_1)$ and $(r_2, t - r_2)$. $-\infty$ if either cell is off the diagonal or a thorn.
- **Transition.** Add the gain of the two cells (once, if the rows match), plus the best of the four predecessors on diagonal $t - 1$. Sort a predecessor's rows before you read it.
- **Base.** $dp[0][0][0] = g[0][0]$. **Answer.** $\max(0,\ dp[2n - 2][n - 1][n - 1])$. **Order.** Increasing $t$.
:::

### Problem: Cherry pickup II {#sec-gd-p4-cherry2}

::: {.p-statement}
Two robots start at the top-left and top-right corners of a grid of non-negative cherries. Each move, both robots drop one row and shift one column left, straight, or right, staying inside the grid. A cell both robots occupy in the same row is collected once. Return the most cherries they can collect by the time they reach the bottom row. Here the grid has at most $70$ rows and $70$ columns.

Source: [LC 1463 · Cherry Pickup II](https://leetcode.com/problems/cherry-pickup-ii/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The problem already synchronises the robots: after $k$ moves both are in row $k$. The state is the row and the two columns. They share a cell exactly when the columns match. A suffix, "most cherries from this row downward", needs no unreachable marker, because every pair of columns is a legal place to be standing. The forward form has to mark the columns a robot cannot yet have reached.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $dp[r][c_1][c_2]$ = most cherries from row $r$ through the bottom, robots standing in columns $c_1$ and $c_2$, current cells included.
- **Transition.** $g[r][c_1] + [c_1 \ne c_2]\, g[r][c_2]$, plus the best of the nine pairs of steps into row $r + 1$ that stay inside the grid.
- **Base.** The bottom row is just the gain. **Answer.** $dp[0][0][\mathrm{cols} - 1]$, the real starts. **Order.** Bottom row upward.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

## Pattern 5: shape DP {#sec-gd-p5}

**From paths to shapes.** Every pattern so far asked about paths that end at a cell. A cell can also anchor a **shape**: the largest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner it is. The transition still reads the cell's neighbours, but the value means a size, not a path.

**Recognise it.** The grid is binary, or a cell is "good" by a local test, and you want the largest axis-aligned square or rectangle, or the number of them. Anchor the shape at one cell. A square is described by one number, the side of the largest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner is that cell. A rectangle is not: fix the bottom row and the problem becomes one histogram per row.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
On a 1-cell,

$$
sq[r][c] = 1 + \min(sq[r-1][c],\ sq[r][c-1],\ sq[r-1][c-1]),
$$

and a 0-cell is $0$. The top row and the left column are $0$ or $1$, since only a $1\times 1$ fits. The answer maximal square asks for is $(\max sq)^2$. The number of all-ones squares is $\sum sq$, because a corner of side $k$ is the corner of $k$ squares.

Column heights are $h[r][c] = h[r-1][c] + 1$ on a 1, and $0$ on a 0. The largest rectangle under one histogram is a monotonic stack, and the stack needs a final bar of height $0$.
:::

**Complexity.** The square recurrence is $O(mn)$ time. One rolling row is $O(n)$ memory, plus a variable that remembers the diagonal the row just overwrote. Heights plus a stack are $O(mn)$ time and $O(n)$ memory: each index is pushed and popped once per row. A prefix-sum check of every rectangle is $O(m^2 n^2)$ and is the oracle, not the submission.

### Problem: Maximal square {#sec-gd-p5-square}

::: {.p-statement}
Given an $m \times n$ matrix of characters `'0'` and `'1'`, return the area of the largest square of ones. Here $m, n \le 300$.

Source: [LC 221 · Maximal Square](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximal-square/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A square of side $k$ with bottom-right corner $(r, c)$ leaves three squares of side $k - 1$: delete the last row, the last column, or both. So the side is one more than the shortest of those three neighbours, and only when $(r, c)$ itself is a one. Up and left cover the two edges. The diagonal covers the interior. Drop the diagonal and `[["0","1"],["1","1"]]` reports area $4$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $sq[r][c]$ = side of the largest all-ones square with bottom-right corner $(r, c)$.
- **Transition.** $0$ if the cell is `'0'`. Otherwise $1 + \min$ of up, left, and diagonal. The border is $1$ when the cell is `'1'`.
- **Answer.** $(\max sq)^2$, which is $0$ when the matrix has no one. **Order.** Reading order. A pad of zeros removes the border case.
:::

def square_rec(matrix):
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])

    def f(r, c):
        if matrix[r][c] == "0":
            return 0
        if r == 0 or c == 0:
            return 1
        return 1 + min(f(r - 1, c), f(r, c - 1), f(r - 1, c - 1))

    best = 0
    for r in range(m):
        for c in range(n):
            best = max(best, f(r, c))
    return best * best

    int m = (int)g.size(), n = (int)g[0].size(), best = 0;

::: {.p-complexity}
**Recursion** is exponential on a block of ones. **Memo**, the **table**, and the **rolling row** are $O(mn)$ time. Memo and the table use $O(mn)$ memory; the rolling row uses $O(n)$, plus one integer for the diagonal. A $300\times 300$ of ones has area $90000$, which fits in a 32-bit integer.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- `[["0"]]` is $0$, not $1$. There is no square.
- `[["1"]]` is $1$. A long row of ones is still area $1$: it is not a square.
- `[["0", "1"], ["1", "0"]]` is $1$. The two ones do not share a corner.
- `[["1", "1", "1"], ["1", "0", "1"], ["1", "1", "1"]]` is $1$. The border is all ones and the centre is a hole, so no $2\times 2$ exists.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Returning the side. The DP value is a side; the problem asks for the area. Sample 1 is $4$, not $2$.
- Forgetting the diagonal neighbour. `[["0", "1"], ["1", "1"]]` becomes area $4$.
- Overwriting the diagonal in the rolling row. `row[c - 1]` is already the new row. Save it in `prev`, and update `prev` on a zero cell too.
- Testing the character as a boolean. `'0'` is not zero; it is the character with code $48$. Compare with `'1'`.
:::

### Problem: Maximal rectangle {#sec-gd-p5-rect}

::: {.p-statement}

int histogram(const vector<int>& h) {
    int n = (int)h.size(), best = 0;
    vector<int> st;
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) {
        int cur = i == n ? 0 : h[i];

            st.pop_back();

**Looking back.** All five patterns fill one table of cells in an order that respects the moves. The climb was about what a cell stores: a count combined with a backward count, a summary of a large predecessor set, a requirement read from the future or a move budget, two positions at once, and finally the size of a shape. Each time the cell alone was not enough, we added the missing fact as an index, exactly as in @sec-od.

## Pattern map

| Signal in the statement | Pattern | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Count paths, or test whether a cell lies on one | Path counting, forward table and backward table | @sec-gd-p1 |
| The move is anywhere in the previous row or column, and you also need the second best | Richer moves | @sec-gd-p2 |
| The start value depends on every prefix of the path | Backward DP, filled from the target | @sec-gd-p3 |
| Four directions, plus a budget of moves, time, or fuel | Layered DP; the counter is the outer loop | @sec-gd-p3-out |
| A move must go to a strictly larger value | Order by value; memoised DFS or a sort | @sec-gd-p3 |
| Two paths, and a shared cell is collected once | Two walkers on one clock | @sec-gd-p4 |
| Go there and come back, right/down then left/up | Two forward walkers, $t = r + c$ | @sec-gd-p4-cherry |
| Both agents drop one row per turn | Row clock, state $(r, c_1, c_2)$ | @sec-gd-p4-cherry2 |
| Largest or number of all-ones squares | Side at the bottom-right corner, minimum of three neighbours | @sec-gd-p5-square |
| Largest all-ones rectangle | Heights per row, histogram, monotonic stack, sentinel $0$ | @sec-gd-p5-rect |
| Four directions and nothing on the walk increases | BFS or Dijkstra, not a table | @sec-gd-p3 |
| Visit every free cell exactly once | The cell is not a state; backtracking | @sec-gd-p5 |

## Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **A forward "need".** Health so far is two numbers, the lowest prefix and the balance. Neither dominates. Dungeon's first sample awards $8$ to the richest path; the answer is $7$ (@sec-gd-p3-dung).
- **The floor of $1$, the seed, and the pad.** $need = \max(1, \min(\text{next}) - \text{cell})$. A missing clamp makes `[[0, 30, -5]]` negative. A seed of $1$ on the princess herself, or a pad of $0$, makes sample 1 return $6$. Outside is $+\infty$ except the one cell past her.
- **The rolling row swept the wrong way.** Dungeon fills right to left, so the right neighbour is already new. Left to right reads the old neighbour. A square's rolling row has the opposite problem: the diagonal was overwritten, and `prev` is the only copy of it (@sec-gd-p5-square).
- **A layer updated in place.** Out-of-boundary paths push every ball to a neighbour. Writing into the same array moves some balls twice in one round. Layer $t + 1$ is a different array (@sec-gd-p3-out).
- **A memo key without the counter.** Ways to leave $(0, 0)$ with one move is $2$; with two moves it is $6$. On a cyclic grid the counter is also what makes the recursion stop.
- **A shared cell paid twice, or impossible stored as $0$.** Cherry pickup sample 1 becomes $8$, and the thorn sample becomes $3$. $-\infty$ is impossible. $\max(0, \cdot)$ happens once, at the public answer (@sec-gd-p4-cherry).
- **The wrong cell of the suffix.** Cherry pickup II's answer is $dp[0][0][\mathrm{cols}-1]$. The maximum of row $0$ lets the robots start anywhere and turns the unreachable $9$ into $9$ (@sec-gd-p4-cherry2).
- **Side versus area, and a histogram with no sentinel.** Maximal square returns the square of the side. Maximal rectangle's row $3, 1, 3, 2, 2$ returns $4$ if the final bar of height $0$ is missing, and the rectangle on that matrix is $6$, not the square's $4$ (@sec-gd-p5-rect).
:::

**2. [H]** [LC 329 · Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-increasing-path-in-a-matrix/){difficulty="Hard"}. Move up, down, left, or right to a strictly larger value. Return the number of cells on the longest such path. ($[[9,9,4],[6,6,8],[2,1,1]] \to 4$.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The value increases, so the cells are a DAG. $len(r, c) = 1 + \max len$ over strictly larger neighbours, or $1$ if there is none. Memoised DFS computes each cell once.

::: {#28a27375 .cell execution_count=113}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def longest_increasing(a):
    m, n = len(a), len(a[0])
    memo = [[0] * n for _ in range(m)]

    def dfs(r, c):
        if memo[r][c]:
            return memo[r][c]
        best = 1
        for dr, dc in ((-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)):
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n and a[nr][nc] > a[r][c]:
                best = max(best, 1 + dfs(nr, nc))
        memo[r][c] = best
        return best

    return max(dfs(r, c) for r in range(m) for c in range(n))

assert longest_increasing([[9, 9, 4], [6, 6, 8], [2, 1, 1]]) == 4
assert longest_increasing([[1]]) == 1

Driving from $i$ to $j \ne i$ costs the absolute difference in fuel. Count routes from `start` to `finish` that use at most `fuel`, modulo $10^9+7$. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Fuel only goes down, so the layer is the fuel still in the tank. Whenever the route stands at `finish`, add it: it may stop, or drive on. A move of cost $0$ cannot happen, because the positions differ.

::: {#c5dbc681 .cell execution_count=114}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def count_routes(locations, start, finish, fuel):
    n = len(locations)
    ways = [[0] * n for _ in range(fuel + 1)]
    ways[fuel][start] = 1
    ans = 0
    for f in range(fuel, -1, -1):
        for i in range(n):
            if ways[f][i] == 0:
                continue
            if i == finish:
                ans = (ans + ways[f][i]) % MOD
            for j in range(n):
                if j == i:
                    continue
                cost = abs(locations[i] - locations[j])
                if cost <= f:
                    ways[f - cost][j] = (ways[f - cost][j] + ways[f][i]) % MOD
    return ans

assert count_routes([2, 3, 6, 8, 4], 1, 3, 5) == 4

A knight starts at `(row, column)` on an $n \times n$ board and makes $k$ moves. Each of the eight moves is equally likely, and a move off the board removes the knight. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The same layered grid as out-of-boundary paths, with probability instead of a count. Each move sends $1/8$ of the mass to every knight neighbour that stays on the board. The answer is the mass remaining after $k$ moves.

::: {#0f34e066 .cell execution_count=115}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def knight_prob(n, k, row, col):
    moves = ((1, 2), (1, -2), (-1, 2), (-1, -2), (2, 1), (2, -1), (-2, 1), (-2, -1))
    cur = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    cur[row][col] = 1.0
    for _ in range(k):
        nxt = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        for r in range(n):
            for c in range(n):
                if cur[r][c] == 0.0:
                    continue
                for dr, dc in moves:
                    nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                    if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n:
                        nxt[nr][nc] += cur[r][c] / 8.0
        cur = nxt
    return sum(sum(line) for line in cur)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The cell is not enough: two paths can arrive with different numbers of neutralisations left. $dp[c][k]$ is the best total at the current row and column $c$ with $k$ neutralisations used. Unreachable stays $-\infty$, because a total may be negative. The counter only grows, so each layer reads itself or the previous row.

::: {#5561ef0f .cell execution_count=116}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def maximum_amount(coins):
    m, n = len(coins), len(coins[0])
    NEG = -10**18
    dp = [[NEG] * 3 for _ in range(n)]
    for r in range(m):
        for c in range(n):
            v = coins[r][c]
            frm = [NEG] * 3
            for k in range(3):
                if r == 0 and c == 0:
                    frm[k] = 0 if k == 0 else NEG
                else:
                    if r > 0:
                        frm[k] = max(frm[k], dp[c][k])
                    if c > 0:
                        frm[k] = max(frm[k], dp[c - 1][k])
            nxt = [NEG] * 3
            for k in range(3):
                best = frm[k] + v if frm[k] != NEG else NEG
                if v < 0 and k > 0 and frm[k - 1] != NEG:
                    best = max(best, frm[k - 1])
                nxt[k] = best
            dp[c] = nxt
    return max(dp[n - 1])

**8. [H]** How many optimal route pairs? Two right/down walkers on an $n \times n$ grid of non-negative values, a shared cell paid once. ($[[1,1],[1,1]] \to 4,\ 2$; all ones $3\times 3 \to 8,\ 6$; $[[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] \to 3,\ 32$; $[[0,3,1],[2,0,4],[1,5,0]] \to 16,\ 2$.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Cherry pickup's clock, with a pair $(best, ways)$ in every cell. A strictly better predecessor replaces the count; a tie adds it. Do not fold $r_1 \le r_2$: swapping the walkers changes an ordered pair.

::: {#076c8402 .cell execution_count=119}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def optimal_pairs(a):
    n = len(a)
    NEG = -10**18
    best = [[NEG] * n for _ in range(n)]
    ways = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    best[0][0] = a[0][0]
    ways[0][0] = 1
    for t in range(1, 2 * n - 1):
        lo, hi = max(0, t - n + 1), min(n - 1, t)
        nb = [[NEG] * n for _ in range(n)]
        nw = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        for r1 in range(lo, hi + 1):
            for r2 in range(lo, hi + 1):
                b, w = NEG, 0
                for d1 in (0, 1):
                    for d2 in (0, 1):
                        p1, p2 = r1 - d1, r2 - d2
                        if p1 < 0 or p2 < 0 or best[p1][p2] == NEG:
                            continue
                        if best[p1][p2] > b:
                            b, w = best[p1][p2], ways[p1][p2]
                        elif best[p1][p2] == b:
                            w = (w + ways[p1][p2]) % MOD
                if b == NEG:
                    continue
                nb[r1][r2] = b + a[r1][t - r1] + (a[r2][t - r2] if r1 != r2 else 0)
                nw[r1][r2] = w
        best, ways = nb, nw
    return best[n - 1][n - 1], ways[n - 1][n - 1]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The child from $(0, 0)$ has exactly $n - 1$ moves and needs $n - 1$ steps on each axis, so it is forced down the main diagonal. The other two stay strictly on opposite sides of that diagonal until the last cell, so they never meet. Each triangle is a one-walker DP. Transpose the grid to reuse it.

::: {#a7b6151d .cell execution_count=120}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def fruits_collected(fruits):
    n = len(fruits)

    def upper(f):
        NEG = -10**18
        prev = [NEG] * n
        prev[n - 1] = f[0][n - 1]
        for r in range(1, n - 1):
            cur = [NEG] * n
            for c in range(r + 1, n):
                best = prev[c]
                if c > 0:
                    best = max(best, prev[c - 1])
                if c + 1 < n:
                    best = max(best, prev[c + 1])
                if best != NEG:
                    cur[c] = best + f[r][c]
            prev = cur
        return prev[n - 1]

    diag = sum(fruits[i][i] for i in range(n))
    tr = [list(col) for col in zip(*fruits)]
    return diag + upper(fruits) + upper(tr)

**10. [M]** Three walkers. Three right/down walkers from $(0, 0)$ to the opposite corner, each cell paid once. On $[[0,1,0,2],[3,0,1,0],[0,2,0,1],[1,0,3,0]]$, two walkers collect $12$. How many do three collect?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The same clock, with rows $r_1 \le r_2 \le r_3$ and eight predecessors. Sort the predecessor's rows before reading them. Equal rows are adjacent after the sort, so the gain adds a cell only when its row differs from the previous walker's. Three walkers collect $13$ of the $14$ on that grid. On the $3\times 4$ greedy grid they collect $6$, which two walkers already collect.

::: {#d8497978 .cell execution_count=121}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def three_walkers(g):
    m, n = len(g), len(g[0])
    NEG = -10**18
    prev = [[[NEG] * m for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    prev[0][0][0] = g[0][0]
    for t in range(1, m + n - 1):
        lo, hi = max(0, t - n + 1), min(m - 1, t)
        cur = [[[NEG] * m for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
        for a in range(lo, hi + 1):
            for b in range(a, hi + 1):
                for c in range(b, hi + 1):
                    best = NEG
                    for mask in range(8):
                        p = [a - (mask & 1), b - ((mask >> 1) & 1), c - ((mask >> 2) & 1)]
                        if min(p) < 0:
                            continue
                        p.sort()
                        best = max(best, prev[p[0]][p[1]][p[2]])
                    if best == NEG:
                        continue
                    gain = g[a][t - a]
                    if b != a:
                        gain += g[b][t - b]
                    if c != b:
                        gain += g[c][t - c]
                    cur[a][b][c] = best + gain
        prev = cur
    return prev[m - 1][m - 1][m - 1]

assert three_walkers([[0, 0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0, 0]]) == 6
assert three_walkers([[0, 1, 0, 2], [3, 0, 1, 0], [0, 2, 0, 1], [1, 0, 3, 0]]) == 13
```

**11. [H]** Paths that never touch. Count the unordered pairs of right/down paths from $(0, 0)$ to $(m - 1, n - 1)$ that share only the two corners. ($2\times 2 \to 1$, $3\times 3 \to 3$, $3\times 4 \to 6$, $4\times 4 \to 20$, $5\times 5 \to 175$.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Synchronise by $t$ and keep the walkers strictly ordered, $r_1 < r_2$, on every diagonal except the first and the last. The finish of that count is the pair of cells just before the corner, $(m - 2, n - 1)$ and $(m - 1, n - 2)$.

::: {#e41d0a06 .cell execution_count=122}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def disjoint_pairs(m, n):
    if m < 2 or n < 2:
        return 0
    prev = [[0] * m for _ in range(m)]
    prev[0][1] = 1
    for t in range(2, m + n - 2):
        lo, hi = max(0, t - n + 1), min(m - 1, t)
        cur = [[0] * m for _ in range(m)]
        for r1 in range(lo, hi + 1):
            for r2 in range(r1 + 1, hi + 1):
                for d1 in (0, 1):
                    for d2 in (0, 1):
                        p1, p2 = r1 - d1, r2 - d2
                        if p1 >= 0 and p1 < p2:
                            cur[r1][r2] += prev[p1][p2]
        prev = cur
    return prev[m - 2][m - 1]

assert [disjoint_pairs(2, 2), disjoint_pairs(3, 3), disjoint_pairs(3, 4), disjoint_pairs(4, 4), disjoint_pairs(5, 5)] == [1, 3, 6, 20, 175]
```

**13. [M]** [LC 764 · Largest Plus Sign](https://leetcode.com/problems/largest-plus-sign/){difficulty="Medium"}. An $n \times n$ grid of ones, except the mines. A plus of order $k$ has four arms of length $k - 1$. Return the largest order. ($n = 5$, mines $[[4,2]] \to 2$; $n = 1$ with its only cell mined $\to 0$.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The order at a cell is the shortest of the four runs of ones that end there. One table, initialised to $n$ and zeroed on mines, takes the minimum with each run as a sweep computes it. A mine stays $0$. A one-cell's run is at least $1$, so reading the table as "is this a one?" stays valid.

::: {#ec33019b .cell execution_count=124}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def plus_sign(n, mines):
    best = [[n] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for r, c in mines:
        best[r][c] = 0
    for i in range(n):
        left = right = up = down = 0
        for j in range(n):
            k = n - 1 - j
            left = left + 1 if best[i][j] else 0
            best[i][j] = min(best[i][j], left)
            right = right + 1 if best[i][k] else 0
            best[i][k] = min(best[i][k], right)
            up = up + 1 if best[j][i] else 0
            best[j][i] = min(best[j][i], up)
            down = down + 1 if best[k][i] else 0
            best[k][i] = min(best[k][i], down)
    return max(max(row) for row in best)

assert plus_sign(5, [[4, 2]]) == 2
assert plus_sign(1, [[0, 0]]) == 0
```

**14. [M]** [LC 1139 · Largest 1-Bordered Square](https://leetcode.com/problems/largest-1-bordered-square/){difficulty="Medium"}. Largest square whose border is all ones; the inside may be anything. Return the number of cells, or $0$. ($[[1,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,1]] \to 9$; $[[1,1,0,0]] \to 1$.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`up` and `left` are the runs ending at the cell. For a bottom-right corner, the bottom and right edges allow sides up to the minimum of those two runs. Try sides downward and accept the first whose top edge and left edge are long enough. A bordered square of side $k$ need not contain one of side $k - 1$.

::: {#127abb9a .cell execution_count=125}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def bordered_square(g):
    m, n = len(g), len(g[0])
    up = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
    left = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
    for r in range(1, m + 1):
        for c in range(1, n + 1):
            if g[r - 1][c - 1]:
                up[r][c] = up[r - 1][c] + 1
                left[r][c] = left[r][c - 1] + 1
    best = 0
    for r in range(1, m + 1):
        for c in range(1, n + 1):
            k = min(up[r][c], left[r][c])
            while k > best:
                if left[r - k + 1][c] >= k and up[r][c - k + 1] >= k:
                    best = k
                    break
                k -= 1
    return best * best

assert bordered_square([[1, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 1]]) == 9
assert bordered_square([[1, 1, 0, 0]]) == 1
```

**15. [M]** [LC 1504 · Count Submatrices With All Ones](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-submatrices-with-all-ones/){difficulty="Medium"}. Count the all-ones rectangles. ($[[1,0,1],[1,1,0],[1,1,0]] \to 13$.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Heights as in maximal rectangle. For each bar, $p$ is the nearest strictly shorter bar on the left. Every rectangle with bottom-right corner $(r, c)$ is either already counted at $p$, or has height exactly $h[c]$ and a left edge in $(p, c]$. That is $cnt[p] + h[c]\cdot(c - p)$.

::: {#0f7d7920 .cell execution_count=126}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def count_submat(mat):
    n = len(mat[0])
    h = [0] * n
    total = 0
    for row in mat:
        for c in range(n):
            h[c] = h[c] + 1 if row[c] else 0
        cnt = [0] * n
        st = []
        for c in range(n):
            while st and h[st[-1]] >= h[c]:
                st.pop()
            p = st[-1] if st else -1
            cnt[c] = (cnt[p] if p >= 0 else 0) + h[c] * (c - p)
            st.append(c)
            total += cnt[c]
    return total

assert count_submat([[1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 0], [1, 1, 0]]) == 13
```

def forest_queries(lines, queries):
    n = len(lines)
    P = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for y in range(1, n + 1):
        for x in range(1, n + 1):
            P[y][x] = (lines[y - 1][x - 1] == "*") + P[y - 1][x] + P[y][x - 1] - P[y - 1][x - 1]
    out = []
    for y1, x1, y2, x2 in queries:
        out.append(P[y2][x2] - P[y1 - 1][x2] - P[y2][x1 - 1] + P[y1 - 1][x1 - 1])
    return out

**17. [M]** Largest square with at most $k$ zeros. Why does $1 + \min$ of three neighbours fail, and what is the side on the maximal-square sample for $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$? (`"10"` / `"01"` with $k = 1 \to 1$.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Three squares with one zero each can frame a square with more than one zero, so the minimum does not add. "Some $s\times s$ square has at most $k$ zeros" is monotone in $s$. Binary-search the side and test every position with a prefix sum of the zeros. The sample gives sides $2, 2, 3, 3$.

::: {#1ddd66ff .cell execution_count=128}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def square_at_most_k(g, k):
    m, n = len(g), len(g[0])
    Z = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
    for i in range(m):
        for j in range(n):
            Z[i + 1][j + 1] = (g[i][j] == "0") + Z[i][j + 1] + Z[i + 1][j] - Z[i][j]

    def ok(s):
        if s == 0:
            return True
        for r in range(s, m + 1):
            for c in range(s, n + 1):
                zeros = Z[r][c] - Z[r - s][c] - Z[r][c - s] + Z[r - s][c - s]
                if zeros <= k:
                    return True
        return False

    lo, hi = 0, min(m, n)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2
        if ok(mid):
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return lo

_G = ["10100", "10111", "11111", "10010"]
assert [square_at_most_k(_G, k) for k in range(4)] == [2, 2, 3, 3]
assert square_at_most_k(["10", "01"], 1) == 1
```
