## Interview questions

**1. Why does a forward DP fail on Dungeon Game, and why is the backward value clamped at $1$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A prefix has two numbers that do not dominate: the lowest health so far, and the health you hold now. "Most health left" on sample 1 follows down, down, right, right, gains $28$, and needs $8$. The answer is $7$. A suffix has one number, the least health on entering it. After the room you must cover the cheaper successor, and you must be alive on entry, so $need = \max(1, \min(\text{next}) - \text{cell})$. Without the floor, `[[0, 30, -5]]` returns a negative (@sec-gd-p3-dung).
:::

**2. What is wrong with a pad of $0$, and with seeding the princess's own cell with $1$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Zero is smaller than every real need, so the minimum walks off the board and skips the rest of the dungeon. Sample 1 returns $6$. The princess's room has a value too: seeding her cell with $1$ ignores the $-5$, and sample 1 again returns $6$. Outside cells are $+\infty$, except the single seed past her room.
:::

**3. Why does the rolling dungeon row run right to left?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`row[c]` still holds the value from the row below, and `row[c + 1]` must already hold the new value to the right. A left-to-right sweep reads the old right neighbour. The square's rolling row is the mirror image of the same idea: you overwrite left to right, and one variable remembers the diagonal you just destroyed (@sec-gd-p5-square).
:::

**4. When do you add a layer instead of reversing the fill?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Reverse the fill when the suffix has a one-number summary and the moves still go only right and down. Add a layer when the moves can go backward, so the cells have a cycle, but some counter — moves, time, fuel, a strictly larger value — increases on every step. The counter, not the cell, is the fill order. If nothing increases, the search is BFS or Dijkstra (@sec-gd-p3-out).
:::

**5. Why is a memo on $(r, c)$ wrong for out-of-boundary paths?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
"Ways to leave $(0, 0)$" is $2$ with one move left and $6$ with two, on the $2\times 2$ sample. A key without the budget returns whichever value was stored first. On a cyclic grid that key also fails to terminate, because a cell calls its neighbour and the neighbour calls it back.
:::

**6. Why are two arrays required for one layer of a four-direction walk?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cells in the same layer do not depend on each other. Every arrow goes to the next value of the counter. Writing the push into the array you are reading lets one ball take several steps in a single round. Sample 2 of out-of-boundary paths stops being $12$.
:::

**7. Why is a round trip two forward walkers, and why is $t = r + c$ enough?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Read the return trip backwards and it is a right/down walk on the same cells. The score is the set of cells, so the direction of the second walk does not matter. Every right or down step increases $r + c$ by one, so after $t$ steps both walkers are on that anti-diagonal and the column is $t - r$. The state is $(t, r_1, r_2)$, not four coordinates (@sec-gd-p4-cherry).
:::

**8. When do two walkers share a cell, and what goes wrong if you add it twice?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A cell $(r, c)$ is visited only at tick $r + c$. Both walkers are there at that tick exactly when their rows match. The gain adds the second cell only when $r_1 \ne r_2$. Adding it always makes sample 1 return $8$: both walkers take the same route and its cherries are paid twice. A $1\times 1$ grid must score its only cell once.
:::

**9. Why is $-\infty$ not $0$, and why does the public answer clamp at $0$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A thorn is unreachable. If that state holds $0$ and is extended like any other state, sample 2 of cherry pickup returns $3$: the walkers cross the thorn diagonal. Keep $-\infty$, and apply $\max(0, \cdot)$ once at the corner, because "no route" is reported as $0$. Do not clamp the intermediate cells: a later cherry cannot rescue a walk that already hit a thorn, and a zero cherry is a real total.
:::

**10. Why is cherry pickup II's answer one entry, not the max of the first row?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The suffix $dp[r][c_1][c_2]$ is "best from here downward", and "here" for the problem is the two starting corners. $dp[0][0][\mathrm{cols}-1]$ is that state. The maximum over row $0$ lets the robots start in any columns. Both official samples still return $24$ and $28$. The grid with a single $9$ that neither robot can reach returns $9$ instead of $0$ (@sec-gd-p4-cherry2).
:::

**11. What does $sq[r][c]$ mean, and why the minimum of three neighbours?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It is the side of the largest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner is $(r, c)$. A square of side $k$ leaves three squares of side $k - 1$ when you delete its last row, its last column, or both, so the side is one more than the shortest of those three, and only if $(r, c)$ is a one. Up and left are the edges. The diagonal is the interior. The problem asks for the area, $(\max sq)^2$ (@sec-gd-p5-square).
:::

**12. Why does the histogram need a bar of height $0$ at the end?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Bars still on the stack have not been measured. Row 2 of the sample is $3, 1, 3, 2, 2$. Without the sentinel the stack still holds the bar of height $1$ and the bar of height $2$, and the area $6$ is never written; the routine returns $4$. The sentinel pops every remaining bar. The width is $i - left - 1$, with $left = -1$ when the stack becomes empty (@sec-gd-p5-rect).
:::

**13. Why is the largest rectangle not the square recurrence?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
One number at a corner cannot name every rectangle that uses that corner: the rectangle's height and width are independent. The square on the sample matrix is $4$. The rectangle is $6$, a $2\times 3$ whose floor is row 2. Fix the bottom row, turn the columns into histogram bars, and solve the histogram.
:::

**14. When is a grid problem not a DP?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When no quantity strictly increases along a move, the cells can contain a cycle and no fill order exists. Path With Minimum Effort is a shortest path. Unique Paths III visits every free cell exactly once, so the state would be the set of visited cells; with at most $20$ cells the intended search is backtracking. A closed walk of odd length on a grid is impossible for a cheaper reason: every edge flips the colour of $r + c$.
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-important title="Five templates"}
- **Path counting.** A forward table from the start and a backward table to the goal. Through one cell the counts multiply, and the cell itself is counted once.
- **Richer moves.** $dp[r][c] = v + \mathrm{opt}$ over a whole previous row or column. Keep the best and the second best so one cell is $O(1)$.
- **Backward and layered.** A requirement decided by the future is filled from the goal, and it is clamped at $1$. A budget of moves, time, or fuel is a layer $(t, r, c)$; layer $t + 1$ is a different array (@sec-gd-p3).
- **Two walkers.** One clock, both free coordinates. A shared cell, $r_1 = r_2$ or $c_1 = c_2$, is collected once. A round trip is two forward walks (@sec-gd-p4).
- **Shape DP.** $sq[r][c] = 1 + \min(\mathrm{up}, \mathrm{left}, \mathrm{diag})$ on a one, and the area is the square of the max. A rectangle is a histogram per row, closed by a bar of height $0$ (@sec-gd-p5).
:::

The first question on any grid is which arrow leaves the cell, and which quantity that arrow increases. That quantity is the fill order. If nothing increases, the algorithm is a search.

A dungeon rolling row runs right to left. A square rolling row runs left to right and keeps the overwritten diagonal in one variable. Two walkers share a cell only on the same tick of the clock, which is why one comparison pays it once. The square on the running matrix is $4$. The rectangle is $6$.

The next chapter leaves the grid. The state becomes a position in a sequence and the value of the last element taken, which is the LIS family, and the first real speed-up is a data structure rather than a shorter table.
